strengths: The paper addresses a useful finite-length coding problem: asymptotically efficient constructions can have substantial redundancy for short sequences. Using learned edit-distance embeddings to guide codebook construction is an interesting application of representation learning.

Algorithm 1 removes neighbors using exact Levenshtein distance. Consequently, its minimum-distance guarantee does not depend on embedding accuracy, and the resulting codebooks support exact single-edit correction with an appropriate decoder.

Table 1 shows consistent improvements over random greedy construction across ten runs, including a 16.8% increase in best codebook cardinality at n=11. Reporting means, variability, maxima, and an ablation of the revised loss provides useful empirical evidence.

The decoding experiments are substantial: querying four neighbors produces zero reported failures in 10^8 trials at each tested length. Synthetic data generation, a source-code repository link, and explicit acknowledgment of approximation and scalability limitations are positive aspects.
weaknesses: The central statistical justification in Section 4.2 is incorrect: batch normalization does not make embeddings jointly Gaussian. Nor does low fitted Gaussian density establish a small Levenshtein neighborhood, particularly after candidates have been removed. The paper needs quantitative evidence connecting its Mahalanobis score to actual neighborhood sizes; the binary t-SNE visualization cannot establish this relationship.

The claimed O(n) decoding complexity is not established. Logarithmic expected k-d-tree search requires assumptions that are not verified for these 64-dimensional embeddings; worst-case queries can scan the codebook. Figure 5 also shows k=1 runtime increasing from 6 to 367 seconds between n=7 and n=11. Furthermore, k=1 has decoding failures, while the more reliable configuration uses verification that the paper itself accounts for as O(n^2).

The decoder comparison is insufficient. Contrary to Section 4.3, full codebook scans are not the only exact option: enumerating possible one-edit corrections and checking codebook membership, or precomputing a received-word lookup table, provides straightforward alternatives in this short-length regime. General edit-distance hardness does not establish hardness of radius-one verification. Without these baselines and memory comparisons, the practical advantage of neural decoding remains unclear.

The codebook comparisons do not adequately establish originality or superiority over strong finite-length search methods. Learned ordering is compared primarily with random ordering, omitting degree-based greedy packing and local-search alternatives. Earlier codebook generation work [17] also needs a closer comparison. Since the embedding architecture and original loss build on [43,44], these comparisons are important for isolating the contribution of the proposed ordering and revised loss.

The near-optimality claim exceeds the evidence. Matching a selected redundancy formula over n=6–11 does not establish proximity to the maximum achievable cardinality, and greedy exhaustion establishes maximality rather than optimality. At n=11, the reported code has approximately 6.85 redundancy bits, versus the basic substitution sphere-packing lower bound of log2(34), approximately 5.09 bits. Tight finite-length bounds or exact optima for smaller cases would make this claim assessable.

Experimental completeness and reproducibility remain limited. Zero sampled failures does not certify correction of every single-edit input, although exhaustive validation is feasible for these codebooks. Tests also assume already isolated segments, leaving boundary recovery and the motivating multiple-error storage setting unvalidated. Despite the repository link, the manuscript omits training sizes, pair sampling, optimization settings, handling of lengths n±1, hardware, and training/codebook-generation costs. These omissions prevent a clear assessment of the method's practical trade-offs.
